questions.q: How often does this lesson say the build-versus-buy decision is made in a typical enterprise?
options: Once, for the whole enterprise, at the time Salesforce is first implemented
It recurs for nearly every new requirement, since there's no universally correct answer that applies to all cases
It is never actually made -- enterprises always default to buying
Only once per fiscal year, during budget planning
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that build-versus-buy recurs constantly, for nearly every new requirement, rather than being settled once for the entire enterprise -- the right call depends on the specific capability's centrality and the maturity of available options.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what is the main payoff of a vendor-consolidation platform strategy, compared to best-of-breed?
options: Every capability always gets the single best available tool regardless of vendor
Fewer integrations to maintain, simpler licensing, a single vendor relationship, and often better internal expertise
Zero ongoing maintenance burden of any kind
Guaranteed lower total licensing cost than any other strategy in all cases
questions.explain: The lesson lists vendor consolidation's payoff as fewer integrations, simpler licensing, a single vendor relationship, and concentrated internal expertise -- at the cost of sometimes not having the single best tool for every individual function.

questions.q: This lesson says an organization that drifts into best-of-breed sprawl without ever deciding to be best-of-breed is an example of what recurring problem from earlier in the course?
options: A dueling systems of record failure specifically
The kind of accidental, undeliberate architecture Chapter 1 warned about -- where a posture should be made explicit rather than drifted into
A classification governance failure
A violation of least privilege
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly connects undeliberate platform-strategy drift to the broader theme, introduced earlier in the course, of accidental architecture that happens by default rather than by an explicit, examined decision.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what three genuinely distinct options should a System Architect evaluate inside a Salesforce-centric enterprise, rather than treating it as a two-option choice?
options: Build natively in Salesforce, buy an AppExchange package, or buy an entirely separate product requiring custom integration
Buy from Salesforce, buy from a competitor, or do nothing at all
Use Flow, use Apex, or use a Trailhead module
Single org, multi-org, or no org at all
questions.explain: The lesson specifically names building natively, buying an AppExchange package, and buying an entirely separate non-Salesforce product with custom integration as three distinct options with different cost and risk profiles, warning against collapsing them into a false two-option choice.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what is a System Architect's actual contribution to a vendor or platform-strategy decision, as distinct from who makes the final call?
options: The architect has sole final authority to select vendors company-wide
A clear-eyed technical assessment of maintenance cost, integration burden, and fit with existing standards, which turns the decision into an informed one rather than a gut call
The architect has no role in vendor decisions whatsoever
The architect's only job is to approve the procurement budget
questions.explain: The lesson states the final authority for vendor/platform strategy typically sits with the governance body, informed by budget and procurement; the architect's contribution is a technical cost/risk/fit assessment that makes the decision an informed one.
